entries.title: Oysters Rockefeller
entries.summary: Oysters on the half shell under a green sauce of puréed herbs and greens, butter and breadcrumbs, baked or glazed until bubbling. Created at Antoine's in 1889, or 1899 by some accounts, it has a secret recipe; every other kitchen makes its own version.
entries.guest: Oysters Rockefeller are baked oysters on the half shell under a rich green herb sauce with butter and breadcrumbs. The dish was first made at Antoine's, in the French Quarter.

paras: Oysters Rockefeller is a dish of oysters on the half shell, opened and served in the deeper of their two shells, each covered with a green sauce and baked, or browned under fierce heat from above, until it bubbles. The sauce is a purée of green herbs and leaves cooked down in butter and bound with breadcrumbs, often lifted with an anise liqueur. Guests everywhere know the name, so every cook and server should be able to describe it and tell its story.
It also teaches the difference between a house original and a style. The original belongs to Antoine's; everything else called Oysters Rockefeller is another kitchen's version.

A common version starts with the greens. Green onions, celery and parsley, with spinach or watercress in many kitchens, are softened in butter, then puréed with fresh breadcrumbs, more butter, hot sauce, salt and a splash of Herbsaint (ERB-sant), the New Orleans anise liqueur, or Pernod, its French cousin, for a faint liquorice note. As a guide, use about 225 g (8 oz) of butter to 450 g (1 lb) of greens and herbs, with 60 g (2 oz) of breadcrumbs for two dozen oysters. Chill the sauce firm so it can be spooned or piped neatly.

Spread a baking tray or the plates with rock salt, the coarse salt sold for ice cream makers, and warm it in the oven. The salt is a bed, not a seasoning: it steadies the round shells so they sit level and keep their juices, and it holds the heat. Nest the shucked oysters, each in its deep shell, in the salt, and cover each to the rim with 15 to 30 ml (1 to 2 tbsp) of sauce.

Bake in a very hot oven, 230 to 260°C (446 to 500°F), for 5 to 10 minutes, the shorter time at the hotter end, or finish under a hot salamander, the kitchen's overhead grill (broiler), set far enough away that the sauce heats through before it browns. It is ready when the sauce bubbles at the edges and the frilled edge of the oyster, the mantle, has just begun to curl. Serve it at once, on its salt.

Pooling butter and a sliding sauce mean the sauce went on warm or had too few crumbs to bind it: chill it firm. A dull olive colour comes from greens cooked too long or a sauce held warm for hours. A watery plate means wet oysters or spinach that was not squeezed dry. A scorched top over a cold oyster means the salamander was too close. And an oyster left in the heat after its edges curl shrinks into a tough button.

Antoine's, opened in 1840 by Antoine Alciatore, credits the dish to his son, Jules. It is usually dated 1889, though some histories, 64 Parishes among them, give 1899, and no record settles it. The story usually told is that Jules wanted a local stand-in for snails, which had grown scarce, and turned to Gulf oysters. He named it for John D. Rockefeller, the oil magnate and one of the richest men in America, because the sauce was so rich. Jules kept the recipe within his kitchen, and the house still does not publish it. Antoine's has said its sauce holds no spinach, the very green most copies reach for.

Tell the story, not the secret: created at Antoine's by Jules Alciatore, in 1889 by most accounts, named for John D. Rockefeller for its richness, and never published. If a guest asks what is in the green sauce, describe the style, herbs and greens, butter, breadcrumbs and usually a touch of anise, and never claim to know Antoine's recipe or call another kitchen's version the original. Warn the guest that the rock salt and shells are very hot, and that the salt is a bed, not for eating.

Questions about how thoroughly the oysters are cooked, or who should avoid oysters, go to the service note and the kitchen. At Brennan's, a guest who wants oysters can be offered the Louisiana Oysters at breakfast and lunch, in a buttery, peppery New Orleans barbecue sauce, or at dinner the Grand Isle Jewel Oysters, served raw, with the raw shellfish advisory from the service note. Confirm at lineup how the Louisiana Oysters are cooked.

faults.fault: Sauce slides off, butter pools in the shell
faults.cause: The sauce went on warm, or had too few breadcrumbs to bind it.
faults.fix: Chill the sauce until firm and add crumbs until it holds a shape on a spoon.

faults.cause: The greens were cooked too long, or the sauce was held warm for hours.
faults.fix: Soften the greens briefly, add the parsley late and chill the sauce quickly.

faults.cause: Wet oysters, or spinach that was not squeezed dry.
faults.fix: Drain the oysters in the shell and squeeze cooked greens hard before puréeing.

faults.fault: Scorched top over a cold oyster
faults.cause: The salamander was too close for a cold sauce.
faults.fix: Lower the rack, or start the oysters in the hot oven and glaze them at the end.

faults.cause: Left in the heat after the edges curled.
faults.fix: Pull them the moment the sauce bubbles and the mantle begins to curl.

cards.front: What is Oysters Rockefeller?
cards.back: Oysters on the half shell under a green sauce of puréed herbs and greens, butter and breadcrumbs, baked or glazed until bubbling.

cards.front: Where was Oysters Rockefeller created, when, and by whom?
cards.back: At Antoine's in New Orleans, by Jules Alciatore, son of the founder, Antoine Alciatore. Most accounts date it to 1889; some, 64 Parishes among them, give 1899.

cards.front: Why is the dish named for John D. Rockefeller?
cards.back: For its richness: the sauce was so rich that it was named for the oil magnate, one of the richest men in America.

cards.front: What can you truthfully say about Antoine's own recipe?
cards.back: Only that it is secret: Antoine's has never published it and says its sauce holds no spinach. Never claim to know it.

cards.front: Which green do most kitchens outside Antoine's use in the sauce?
cards.back: Spinach, usually with green onion, celery and parsley, lifted with an anise liqueur such as Herbsaint or Pernod.

cards.front: What is Herbsaint, and what does it bring to the sauce?
cards.back: A New Orleans anise liqueur, said ERB-sant; a splash gives the sauce its faint liquorice note. Pernod is the French stand-in.

cards.front: Why are the oysters baked and served on rock salt?
cards.back: The coarse salt steadies the round shells so they sit level and keep their juices, and it holds the heat to the table.

cards.front: How do you know the oysters are ready to leave the heat?
cards.back: The sauce bubbles at the edges and the frilled edge of the oyster has just begun to curl; longer, and the oyster shrinks and toughens.

cards.front: Why is the green sauce chilled before it goes on the oysters?
cards.back: A firm, cold sauce can be spooned or piped neatly and stays on the oyster; a warm one slides off and leaves pools of butter.

cards.front: What is a salamander, and what does it do for this dish?
cards.back: The kitchen's overhead grill (broiler): fierce heat from above that glazes the sauce until it bubbles, set far enough away to heat it through.

cards.front: How should a server tell a guest the Rockefeller story?
cards.back: Give the house's story, Jules Alciatore at Antoine's, named for Rockefeller's riches, and describe the style; never claim to know Antoine's secret recipe.

cards.front: A Brennan's guest loves Oysters Rockefeller. Which of our oysters can you offer?
cards.back: At breakfast and lunch, the Louisiana Oysters in a buttery, peppery New Orleans barbecue sauce; at dinner, the raw Grand Isle Jewels, with the raw shellfish advisory from the service note. Confirm at lineup how the Louisiana Oysters are cooked.

questions.answer: It steadies the shells and holds heat

It draws water out of the sauce
It stops the shells opening in the oven

questions.answer: Bubbling sauce, edges just curling

The sauce turns black on top

questions.why: Bubbling edges mean the sauce is hot through, and a curling mantle means the oyster is just cooked; past that point it shrinks and toughens.

questions.q: Why is the green sauce chilled firm before it is spread on the oysters?
questions.answer: So it stays on the oyster

So the anise flavour mellows first
So the oyster stays raw inside
questions.why: A cold, firm sauce can be spooned or piped neatly and melts onto the oyster in the oven; a warm one slides off and pools as butter.

entries.title: Oysters Bienville
entries.summary: Baked oysters under a thick, rich sauce of shrimp, mushrooms, green onion and garlic, bound with roux and cream and enriched with yolk, finished with sherry, crumbs and cheese. Named for the founder of New Orleans, and claimed by two old houses.
entries.guest: Oysters Bienville are baked on the half shell under a creamy sauce of chopped shrimp, mushrooms and sherry, with a golden crust of breadcrumbs and cheese.

paras: Oysters Bienville is the other great baked oyster of the old New Orleans houses. Where Rockefeller is green and herbal, Bienville is ivory and rich: oysters on the half shell, each buried under a thick sauce of chopped shrimp, mushrooms, green onion and garlic, bound with a roux, flour cooked in butter, and milk or cream, enriched with egg yolk and sharpened with sherry, then crusted with breadcrumbs and cheese and baked until golden. The test for a cook is a sauce that stands on a hot oyster without running, yet eats creamy.

Shuck the oysters first, keep them chilled in their deep shells and strain their liquor, the salty juice from the shells. Sweat chopped green onion and garlic in butter without colour, add finely chopped mushrooms and cook until their water has gone, then stir in the flour and cook the roux for 2 to 3 minutes so it loses its raw taste. Whisk in warm, not hot, milk or cream a little at a time, with the oyster liquor, and simmer until very thick. Season with salt, white pepper and cayenne.

Off the heat, temper the yolks: whisk a ladle of hot sauce into them, then stir them back in. With this much roux the yolk is shielded, as it is in a pastry cream, so the sauce can come back to a gentle simmer for a minute; keep stirring so the thick sauce does not catch and scorch on the bottom. Then fold in the chopped cooked shrimp and a splash of dry sherry, so the shrimp only warm through and stay tender.

Spread the sauce in a tray, press cling film onto it and chill it firm, at least 2 hours. Pour off any liquor the oysters have given up since; some kitchens part-bake them for a minute and drain off the water that runs out. Nest the shells in hot rock salt, mound cold sauce over each oyster to the rim, and scatter it with breadcrumbs, grated Parmesan or Romano and a pinch of paprika. Bake at about 230°C (446°F) for 10 to 15 minutes, until bubbling and golden, with a moment under the salamander if it needs colour.

Take away the shrimp, mushrooms and sherry and what is left is a béchamel, milk thickened with a white roux, made about twice as thick as usual and enriched with yolk. That makes the Bienville sauce a New Orleans cousin in the béchamel family: a rich white sauce with a garnish, baked and browned like a gratin, a dish finished under a golden crust. Some kitchens use seafood stock and the oyster liquor in place of milk, which moves it towards velouté, a stock thickened with roux.

A sauce that floods the shell was too thin or went on warm: cook it thicker and chill it firm. A watery puddle under the crust comes from undrained oysters or mushrooms not cooked dry. A lumpy sauce had its liquid added too fast or too hot; shreds of cooked yolk mean the yolks went in untempered. A pasty, floury taste means the roux was not cooked out. A pale top needs a hotter oven or the salamander; a scorched top over a cold middle means the heat was too close. An oyster baked past the moment its edges curl turns small and tough.

The dish is named for Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne, Sieur de Bienville, the French officer, born in New France at what is now Montreal, who founded New Orleans in 1718 and governed the colony of Louisiana. Bienville Street in the French Quarter carries his name, and Arnaud's stands on it.

Who made it first is disputed. Arnaud's is the house most often linked with the dish, and some accounts credit its founder, Arnaud Cazenave. Antoine's claims it for its own kitchen, and other accounts say it began there and Arnaud's made it famous. No record settles it, so a server says that both houses claim it and picks no side.

Describe it plainly: oysters baked under a creamy sauce of chopped shrimp, mushrooms, green onion and sherry, with a golden crust of crumbs and cheese. Beside Rockefeller, it is the creamy one; Rockefeller is the green one. Say it BEE-en-vil. Warn the guest that the rock salt and shells are hot. Recipes vary from house to house, so any allergy or dietary question goes to the kitchen, never answered from memory.

faults.fault: Sauce runs off and floods the shell
faults.cause: Too little roux, or the sauce went on warm.
faults.fix: Cook it to about twice the thickness of a medium béchamel and chill it firm before building.

faults.cause: Oysters not drained, or mushrooms not cooked dry.
faults.fix: Pour off the liquor, part-bake and drain the oysters if needed, and cook the mushrooms until dry.

faults.cause: The liquid went into the roux too fast or too hot, without steady whisking.
faults.fix: Add warm liquid a little at a time, whisking each addition smooth, and whisk hard at the first sign of a lump.

faults.cause: The yolks went straight into the hot sauce untempered and set before they could disperse.
faults.fix: Temper them with a ladle of hot sauce first and stir them in at once; once shreds form they stay.

faults.cause: The roux was not cooked out before the liquid went in.
faults.fix: Cook the roux for 2 to 3 minutes, then simmer the sauce until it tastes clean.

faults.fault: Pale top, or a scorched top over a cold middle
faults.cause: An oven too cool, or a thick, cold mound under heat that was too close.
faults.fix: Bake in a hot oven until bubbling, then glaze briefly under the salamander.

cards.front: What goes into the Bienville sauce?
cards.back: Chopped shrimp, mushrooms, green onion and garlic in a thick roux sauce of milk or cream, enriched with yolk and finished with sherry.

cards.front: What goes on top of the sauce before baking?
cards.back: Breadcrumbs mixed with grated cheese such as Parmesan or Romano, often with a pinch of paprika, to brown into a crust.

cards.front: Who is Oysters Bienville named for?
cards.back: Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne, Sieur de Bienville, the French officer, born in New France at what is now Montreal, who founded New Orleans in 1718 and governed Louisiana.

cards.front: Who created Oysters Bienville?
cards.back: Disputed: Arnaud's is the house most often linked with it, some crediting its founder, Arnaud Cazenave, and Antoine's claims it too. Teach both claims and pick no side.

cards.front: Where does the Bienville sauce sit among the classic sauces?
cards.back: In the béchamel family: a thick roux and milk sauce enriched with yolk, a New Orleans cousin with a shrimp and mushroom garnish.

cards.front: Why is the Bienville sauce made about twice as thick as a medium béchamel?
cards.back: It must stand in a mound on a hot oyster without running; a thinner sauce floods the shell in the oven.

cards.front: Why is the sauce chilled firm before the oysters are built?
cards.back: Cold and firm, it can be mounded neatly and holds its shape while the oven heats it through and browns the crust.

cards.front: How do the yolks go into the hot sauce without scrambling?
cards.back: Temper them: whisk a ladle of hot sauce into the yolks, then stir them back in. With this much roux the sauce can then simmer without curdling, stirred so it does not scorch.

cards.front: Why are the oysters drained, or briefly part-baked, before the sauce goes on?
cards.back: Oysters give up water as they heat, and raw mushrooms hold plenty; drain the oysters and cook the mushrooms dry, or a watery pool forms under the crust.

cards.front: How does a server tell Bienville from Rockefeller at the table?
cards.back: Bienville is the creamy one, shrimp, mushroom and sherry under a cheese crust; Rockefeller is the green herb sauce.

The tomato family

questions.q: Why is the Bienville sauce cooked far thicker than a pouring sauce?

distractors: So the sherry flavour stays sharper
So the oysters cook more quickly
So the shrimp cook through in the oven
questions.why: The sauce has to hold its shape over an oyster in a hot oven; with a thinner roux it runs off and floods the shell.

questions.q: The Bienville sauce turned grainy, with shreds of cooked yolk, once the yolks went in. What happened?

distractors: The roux was cooked too long
The sherry went in too early
The mushrooms were chopped too fine
questions.why: Yolk dropped straight into a thick, very hot sauce sets in shreds before it can disperse. Tempered first, it blends in smoothly, and with this much roux the sauce can then simmer, as a pastry cream does.

questions.q: A watery pool forms under the Bienville crust. What is the likely cause?
questions.answer: Wet oysters or raw mushrooms
distractors: An oven that was much too hot
Cheese grated too fine for the crust
A sauce with too much roux in it
questions.why: Oysters give up water as they heat and raw mushrooms hold plenty, so the oysters are drained and the mushrooms cooked dry.

questions.q: What forms the golden crust on Oysters Bienville?

Puréed parsley and spinach
Crushed pecans and brown sugar
questions.why: Crumbs and cheese such as Parmesan or Romano brown in the hot oven over the creamy sauce; the green purée belongs to Rockefeller.

questions.q: A guest asks how Bienville differs from Rockefeller. What is the plain answer?

Bienville is green; Rockefeller is creamy
questions.why: Both are oysters baked on the half shell; Bienville carries a creamy shrimp, mushroom and sherry sauce, Rockefeller a green herb sauce.

entries.title: Shrimp rémoulade and Shrimp Arnaud
entries.summary: Chilled boiled Gulf shrimp dressed in a sharp Creole rémoulade on shredded lettuce, a starter of the old New Orleans houses. Shrimp Arnaud is Arnaud's own version, in its red rémoulade, and the house's signature starter.
entries.guest: Shrimp rémoulade is chilled Gulf shrimp in a tangy, peppery sauce of Creole mustard, paprika and horseradish, on crisp shredded lettuce.

paras: Shrimp rémoulade (REM-uh-lahd) is a cold starter: Gulf shrimp boiled in seasoned water, chilled hard, dressed in the New Orleans rémoulade and piled on shredded iceberg lettuce. It has long been a fixture of the old Creole houses, a cold, sharp opening before the rich dishes that follow. Shrimp Arnaud is Arnaud's own version: the same idea in the house's red rémoulade, and the starter the house is known for. For a cook the dish is two jobs done with care: shrimp cooked tender and chilled fast, and a sauce that is bright, hot and cold.

Cook the shrimp in a court-bouillon, a short, seasoned broth made for the purpose: water salted like the sea, about 30 g (1 oz) of salt to 1 litre (about 1 quart), with lemon, bay, onion, celery and cayenne or a crab boil seasoning, simmered for about 15 minutes to draw out the flavour. Bring it back to the boil, add the shrimp, shell on for more flavour, and let it return to a bare simmer.

Medium shrimp take 2 to 3 minutes: they are done when the flesh turns opaque and they curl into a loose C. A tight O means they went too long and will be tough. Some cooks cut the heat as the shrimp go in and let them steep for 3 to 5 minutes, which seasons them more and cooks them more gently.

Chill them fast. Lift the shrimp straight into an ice bath, roughly equal parts ice and water, salted a little so it does not wash out the seasoning, and leave them until cold right through. Fast chilling stops the cooking, keeps the flesh firm and moves the shrimp quickly through the warm temperatures in which bacteria grow. Drain them, peel and devein them, taking out the dark gut along the back, pat them dry and keep them covered at 5°C (41°F) or below. Wet shrimp water down the sauce.

Shred iceberg lettuce fine and keep it cold and dry. Toss the shrimp in the rémoulade close to service, or let them soak in it in the fridge if the house likes them that way; never dress the lettuce ahead, or it wilts. Pile the lettuce on a chilled plate, set the shrimp on top, spoon over a little more sauce and add a lemon wedge.

Every house makes its own rémoulade, and the versions fall into two camps. The red style is a dressing with no mayonnaise: Creole mustard, a coarse, vinegary whole-grain mustard, paprika, horseradish, lemon or vinegar and oil whisked together, brick red, sharp and hot, led by the mustard. The pink style is built on mayonnaise with the same seasonings stirred in, creamier and milder, led by the mayonnaise. Shrimp Arnaud belongs to the red camp. The first thing to learn on joining a kitchen is which camp the house is in. The sauce itself has its own entry.

Tough, rubbery shrimp curled into a tight O were overcooked: pull them at a loose C and chill them at once. Bland shrimp came from a liquor that was under-salted or not simmered before they went in. Soft, mushy shrimp were past their best, thawed in warm water or refrozen, or sat too long in a salty or acid dressing. A watery sauce and limp lettuce mean wet shrimp or lettuce dressed too early: dry everything and dress at the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen.

Describing the sauce is the server's job: tangy and peppery, coloured with paprika, sharp with Creole mustard, with the nose-tingling heat of horseradish and the crunch of finely chopped celery and green onion. Warn a guest who expects a mild, tartar-like sauce that this one has heat. Say the name REM-uh-lahd; RUM-uh-lahd is heard in New Orleans too.

Questions about egg in a pink rémoulade, about mustard or about shellfish go to the kitchen, never answered from memory. At Brennan's, a guest meets rémoulade as the chive rémoulade with the Crawfish Meat Pies, a snack on the Bubbles at Brennan's list in the Roost Bar and the courtyard; the menu does not print its recipe, so its style is a question for the kitchen too.

cards.back: Arnaud's own shrimp rémoulade, made with the house's red rémoulade, and the house's signature starter.

cards.front: What separates a red rémoulade from a pink one?
cards.back: Red is a dressing with no mayonnaise, led by Creole mustard and paprika in oil; pink is built on mayonnaise, creamier and milder.

cards.front: What do the shrimp for rémoulade cook in?
cards.back: A court-bouillon: water salted like the sea, with lemon, bay, onion, celery and cayenne or crab boil, simmered first to flavour it.

cards.front: How do you know a boiled shrimp is done?
cards.back: The flesh turns opaque and it curls into a loose C, after 2 to 3 minutes for medium shrimp; a tight O means it is overcooked.

cards.front: Why do the shrimp go straight into an ice bath?
cards.back: It stops the cooking at once, keeps the flesh firm and chills it quickly through the warm temperatures where bacteria grow.

cards.front: How are the cooked shrimp held before service?
cards.back: Peeled, deveined, patted dry and covered at 5°C (41°F) or below, so they stay firm and do not water down the sauce.

cards.front: Why is the shredded lettuce never dressed ahead?
cards.back: The sauce wilts it within minutes; the lettuce is there cold and crisp, to cool the heat of the sauce.

cards.front: How do you describe the rémoulade to a guest?
cards.back: Tangy and peppery: paprika for colour, Creole mustard and horseradish for sharpness and heat, celery and green onion for crunch.

cards.front: How is rémoulade said in the dining room?
cards.back: REM-uh-lahd; RUM-uh-lahd is also heard in New Orleans, so either will be understood.

cards.front: Where does a Brennan's guest meet rémoulade?
cards.back: As the chive rémoulade with the Crawfish Meat Pies, on the Bubbles at Brennan's list in the Roost Bar and courtyard; which style it is, and what is in it, are questions for the kitchen.

questions.q: Shrimp Arnaud is dressed in which style of rémoulade?
questions.answer: A red rémoulade, led by mustard
distractors: A pink rémoulade built on mayonnaise
A white French rémoulade with capers
A ketchup cocktail sauce with horseradish
questions.why: Shrimp Arnaud is the house's own shrimp rémoulade in its red, mustard-led sauce; the pink style is built on mayonnaise and the French one is white.

questions.q: What mainly separates a pink rémoulade from a red one?
questions.answer: The pink is built on mayonnaise
distractors: The pink uses cooked tomato purée
The pink has no mustard at all
The pink is served warm
questions.why: Both carry Creole mustard, paprika and horseradish; the red is an oil and mustard dressing, the pink a mayonnaise with those seasonings stirred in.

questions.q: Which shape tells you a boiled shrimp is cooked just right?
questions.answer: A loose C
distractors: A tight O
Straight and flat
Split along the back
questions.why: As the flesh turns opaque the shrimp curls into a loose C; keep cooking and it tightens into an O and turns rubbery.

questions.q: Why are the boiled shrimp moved straight into an ice bath?
questions.answer: To stop the cooking and chill them
distractors: To loosen the sauce before dressing
To wash off the seasoning
To soften the shells for eating
questions.why: Left warm, shrimp keep cooking and toughen; ice water stops them at once and takes them quickly through the temperatures where bacteria grow.

questions.q: How cold should the cooked shrimp be held for service?
questions.answer: 5°C (41°F) or below
distractors: 10°C (50°F) or below
20°C (68°F), room temperature
Held warm at 57°C (135°F)
questions.why: Cold food is held at 5°C (41°F) or below; covered and dry, the shrimp stay firm and keep the sauce from watering down.

questions.q: Why is the shredded lettuce for shrimp rémoulade never dressed ahead?
questions.answer: The sauce wilts it within minutes
distractors: The lettuce turns bitter in the acid
The mustard loses its colour
The sauce sets solid on the plate
questions.why: Shredded iceberg goes limp under the sauce in minutes, and the cold, crisp lettuce is what cools the heat of the rémoulade.

questions.q: How should the water for boiling rémoulade shrimp be seasoned?
questions.answer: Salted like the sea, with lemon and spice
distractors: Left plain, with no salt at all
Lightly salted, so the shrimp stay sweet
Sweetened with sugar instead of salt
questions.why: The shrimp take their seasoning from the court-bouillon, so it is salted well and simmered with lemon, bay, aromatics and cayenne first.

questions.q: Which ingredients give a Creole rémoulade its sharp heat?
questions.answer: Creole mustard and horseradish
distractors: Chopped celery and green onion
Mayonnaise and fresh lemon juice
Capers and chopped gherkins
questions.why: Coarse Creole mustard and prepared horseradish bring the sharp, nose-tingling heat, with paprika for colour and celery for crunch.

entries.title: Trout meunière and amandine at Galatoire's
entries.say: TROWT muhn-YEHR and ah-mahn-DEEN at GAL-uh-twahrz
entries.summary: Speckled trout, the Gulf's delicate spotted sea trout, floured and fried or sautéed, then covered with a dark New Orleans brown butter meunière and toasted almonds: Galatoire's trout meunière amandine, a classic of the Bourbon Street house.
entries.guest: At Galatoire's the trout comes floured and fried golden, under a dark, nutty brown butter sauce sharpened with lemon and scattered with toasted almonds.

paras: On the old New Orleans menus, trout means speckled trout, the spotted sea trout of the Gulf's bays and marshes. Despite the name it is no true trout: it belongs to the drum family, with redfish, and has soft, white, sweet flesh with a fine flake. The dish to know is the one Galatoire's made its own, trout meunière amandine: a fillet floured and fried or sautéed until golden, covered with a dark brown butter sauce, the meunière, and scattered with toasted sliced almonds. It joins two French ideas, à la meunière and amandine, on one plate.

Trim the fillets, skin off, and feel for pin bones, the fine bones along the centre line. Pat them dry and season them; just before they go in, dip them in milk or an egg wash, then dredge them in seasoned flour and shake off the excess; the flour browns into a golden crust and holds the delicate flesh together. Fry in oil at about 175°C (347°F), or sauté in clarified butter, butter with its milk solids removed, or oil in a hot pan for 2 to 3 minutes a side, turning once with a wide fish slice. Drain on a rack, never on paper, so the crust stays crisp.

Toast sliced almonds in a dry pan or a 160°C (320°F) oven for 5 to 8 minutes, until golden and fragrant; they burn quickly. For the meunière, cook butter over medium heat. It melts, foams as its water boils off, and its milk solids sink and brown. Take it past the hazelnut colour of the French beurre noisette to a deep brown with a strong, toasty smell, then pull it off the heat and add lemon juice, which hisses and spits, so stand back. Season it, add the almonds and spoon both over the fish at once.

The French à la meunière, the miller's wife's way, is lighter: the floured fish is cooked in butter, sprinkled with lemon juice and chopped parsley, and covered with foaming beurre noisette, butter browned only to a hazelnut gold. The New Orleans meunière goes darker and richer, browned further and sharpened with lemon, and in some houses built up with stock and seasonings into a fuller brown sauce. Each house keeps its own build, and Galatoire's has its own: teach the method, and describe the house's dish only as the house does. Amandine adds toasted almonds.

A soggy, greasy crust means oil that was too cool or a crowded pan. A coating that peels away means the fish was floured too long before cooking or turned before its crust had set. Butter taken past deep brown to black is bitter and cannot be saved: pour it out and start again. A fillet that breaks was handled roughly or turned more than once, and speckled trout forgives neither. Pale, soft almonds were not toasted long enough.

Galatoire's opened on Bourbon Street in 1905, founded by Jean Galatoire, and trout meunière amandine has long been one of its signature dishes. Trout Marguery, long a house speciality, is the other classic: trout under a rich, yolk-thickened sauce in the hollandaise family, with shrimp, named for sole Marguery, the dish of a Paris restaurant of that name. Together they show how the old menus dressed a delicate fish: meunière, amandine, Marguery, or crowned with lump crabmeat.

Ordering at Galatoire's has its own customs. For most of its history the downstairs dining room took no reservations, and on Fridays the line on Bourbon Street formed long before a lunch that runs well into the afternoon. The upstairs rooms now take reservations; how the downstairs room books today, Friday lunch included, is worth checking on the house's own site before you tell a guest. Regulars keep their own waiter for years and often order by asking what is good today.

Describe it as a delicate Gulf fish, floured and fried golden, under a dark, nutty brown butter with lemon and toasted almonds. Every nut or allergy question goes to the kitchen. At Brennan's, the nearest plate is the Pecan Gulf Fish at breakfast and lunch: the Gulf fish of the day topped with lump crab, with a pecan bordelaise; learn the day's fish, how it is cooked and which bordelaise it is at lineup.

ratios.label: Meunière for two portions
ratios.value: About 115 g (4 oz) of butter to 1 tbsp (15 ml) of lemon juice

ratios.label: Almonds for each portion
ratios.value: About 30 g (1 oz) of sliced almonds, toasted

ratios.label: A thin fillet in the pan
ratios.value: 2 to 3 minutes a side, turned once

temps.label: Frying oil for the floured fillets

faults.cause: Oil too cool, or too many fillets in the pan at once.
faults.fix: Heat the oil to about 175°C (347°F) and cook in batches so it stays hot.

faults.cause: The fish was not patted dry before the milk dip, the flour sat on it until it turned gummy, or it was turned before the crust set.
faults.fix: Pat the fillets dry, dip and dredge just before they go in, shake off the excess and leave them until the crust sets before turning once.

faults.cause: Browned past deep brown into burnt.
faults.fix: Pour it out and start again, pulling the pan off the heat as soon as it smells toasty.

faults.cause: Delicate speckled trout handled roughly or turned more than once.
faults.fix: Turn it once with a wide fish slice and lift it straight onto the plate.

faults.cause: Not toasted long enough.
faults.fix: Toast them until golden and fragrant, shaking often and watching closely.

cards.front: What fish is behind the New Orleans trout dishes?
cards.back: Speckled trout, the spotted sea trout of the Gulf: a member of the drum family, not a true trout, with soft, sweet white flesh.

cards.front: What is Galatoire's trout meunière amandine?
cards.back: A trout fillet floured and fried or sautéed golden, covered with a dark brown butter meunière sharpened with lemon, and toasted sliced almonds.

cards.front: Why is the trout floured before it is cooked?
cards.back: The flour browns into a golden crust and holds the soft, flaky flesh together in the pan.

cards.front: How does the New Orleans meunière differ from the French one?
cards.back: It is darker and richer: the butter goes past hazelnut to deep brown, sharpened with lemon, and some houses build it fuller still.

cards.front: What is the French à la meunière finish?
cards.back: Lemon juice and chopped parsley over the cooked fish, then foaming beurre noisette, butter browned only to a hazelnut gold.

cards.front: When does the lemon go into the browned butter, and why with care?
cards.back: Off the heat, once the butter is brown; it stops the browning, but it hisses and spits, so stand back.

cards.front: How are the almonds prepared for amandine?
cards.back: Sliced almonds toasted in a dry pan or a 160°C (320°F) oven until golden and fragrant, watched closely because they burn fast.

cards.front: What should a cook or server say about Galatoire's meunière recipe?
cards.back: That the house has its own build: teach the method, describe Galatoire's dish only as the house does, and never claim to know its recipe.

cards.front: What is trout Marguery?
cards.back: A long-standing Galatoire's speciality: trout under a rich, yolk-thickened sauce in the hollandaise family, with shrimp, named for the Paris sole Marguery.

cards.front: What is the Friday lunch at Galatoire's?
cards.back: A long lunch that runs into the afternoon; for most of its history the downstairs room took no reservations, so the line on Bourbon Street formed early.

cards.front: What is the waiter tradition at Galatoire's?
cards.back: Regulars keep their own waiter for years and often order by asking what is good today rather than reading the menu.

cards.front: A guest asks about nuts in the trout amandine. What do you do?
cards.back: Say it is finished with toasted almonds and send every nut or allergy question to the kitchen.

questions.q: Speckled trout, the fish of the New Orleans trout dishes, belongs to which family?
questions.answer: The drum family
distractors: The salmon and trout family
The flounder family
The catfish family
questions.why: The spotted sea trout is a drum, a cousin of redfish, and only shares a name with the freshwater trout of the salmon family.

questions.q: What finishes Galatoire's trout meunière amandine?
questions.answer: Brown butter, lemon and almonds
distractors: Hollandaise-style sauce with shrimp
A red wine sauce with shallots
Tomato sauce with capers and olives
questions.why: Meunière is the brown butter and lemon, amandine the toasted almonds; the hollandaise-style sauce with shrimp belongs to trout Marguery.

questions.q: How does the New Orleans meunière usually differ from the French one?
questions.answer: It is browned darker and richer
distractors: It is made with olive oil, not butter
It is thickened with egg yolk
It is served cold
questions.why: The French beurre noisette stops at hazelnut gold; New Orleans takes the butter to a deep brown, and some houses build it fuller still.

questions.q: When is lemon juice added to the meunière butter?
questions.answer: Off the heat, once it is brown
distractors: Before the butter has started to melt
While the butter is still foaming
After the sauce has gone cold
questions.why: Lemon stops the browning at the colour you want, and off the heat its hiss and spit are easier to manage.

questions.q: Trout Marguery, long on the Galatoire's menu, comes under which sauce?
questions.answer: A rich hollandaise-style sauce with shrimp
distractors: Brown butter with toasted pecans and lemon
A green purée of herbs, spinach and anise
A cold red rémoulade with celery and mustard
questions.why: Trout Marguery, named for the Paris sole Marguery, is sauced richly with yolk and shrimp, unlike the brown butter dishes.

questions.q: A guest asks for Galatoire's meunière recipe. What is the right answer?
questions.answer: The house's own; describe the method
distractors: It is brown butter with Worcestershire
It is the Escoffier recipe, unchanged
It is a roux sauce made with veal stock
questions.why: Every house keeps its own meunière, so a server describes brown butter and lemon and never claims to know Galatoire's build.

questions.q: What marks the Friday lunch at Galatoire's?
questions.answer: A long lunch and, by tradition, a line
distractors: A set menu served only to members
A jazz brunch with a buffet
A tasting menu booked months in advance
questions.why: For most of its history the downstairs room took no reservations, so the Bourbon Street line formed early, and the lunch runs well into the afternoon.

questions.q: Why is the trout dredged in flour before it is fried or sautéed?
questions.answer: For a crust that holds it together
distractors: To thicken the brown butter sauce
To stop the almonds sticking
To keep the fish white all the way through
questions.why: Speckled trout is soft and flaky, and the flour coat browns into a crust that protects it and keeps it whole in the pan.
